Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Swindon Man in Swindon charged with assisting Russian intelligence agency Joshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing London Raphael Boyd Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.10 EDT First published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man has been charged with offences related to national security as part of an ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing (CTP) London, according to the Metropolitan police. Joshua Cammidge, 31, was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday 4 September by CTP London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire police. Searches were also carried out at a different address in Swindon. He was further arrested and detained the following day, being charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and intending to commit or engage in conduct to prepare an act of sabotage. The Met have claimed that Cammidge’s arrests relate to alleged contact with a representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency that have been accused of previously engaging in acts of sabotage against Britain and its allies. The National Security Act, which Cammidge was arrested and charged under, was introduced in 2023 to help increase the measures that law enforcement can take in order to protect the UK from security threats such as espionage, foreign interference or influence, and sabotage. Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Joshua Cammidge with National Security Act offences following a counter-terrorism policing investigation. “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings. “We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial. “It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.” Cammidge will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday 10 September. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8r.text: Image source, Saycheese Image caption, Ben Dancer reached his target early on Tuesday morning - and kept dancing for another nine hours By Makuochi Okafor BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lagos Published 28 September 2026 Updated 2 hours ago A Nigerian dancer has completed a 168-hour dance marathon in Lagos in a bid to set a new world record. Benjamin Daniel, known as "Ben Dancer", aimed to dance for seven days to break the Guinness World Records title for the longest dance marathon by an individual. Cheered on by friends and supporters at Lagos's Freedom Park, the 33-year-old reached his target time at around 03:00 local time but continued dancing for another nine hours until midday, his team says. The physically exhausted dancer has now gone to hospital for a medical check-up. Guinness World Records has confirmed to the BBC that it has received Daniel's application for the title. The current record stands at 127 hours. "Benjamin's application is active and we now eagerly await submission of his evidence, which will then go through our official review and verification process before any record can be confirmed," a spokesperson for Guinness World Records said in the statement. His team said they were "elated" and emotional after watching him complete the challenge, which has been live streamed on social media. Young people gathered in recent days to cheer him on at Freedom Park in Lagos, filming his every move and dancing along from behind the barriers. "It's a beautiful moment. Seeing how far he has come and witnessing him achieve this feat made me incredibly proud and grateful to God," Uche Anumudu, one of those watching, told the BBC. The current record was set by Indian dancer Srushti Sudhir Jagtap in 2023, when she was 16. Her performance focused mainly on kathak, one of India's major classical dance forms. Ben Dancer, who has been dancing professionally for 18 years and began his attempt last Tuesday, drew on Nigeria's rich dance traditions as well as its fast-changing internet culture. Afrobeats was a constant presence during his performance, alongside genres including fuji, jazz and zouk. At times, he swapped his dance clothes for traditional Nigerian outfits, including the flowing agbada and dashiki. Image source, Saycheese Image caption, Ben Dancer was allowed to rest for five minutes every hour Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, with a wide range of cultural traditions. Ben Dancer's team says the performance was intended to reflect that diversity, rather than simply test his physical endurance. He underwent intensive fitness training before the attempt, changing his diet and focusing on carbohydrates and cardiovascular conditioning. During the danceathon, he ate lightly and drank fluids while taking the permitted five minutes of rest for every continuous hour of activity. He chose to dance for several hours at a time before taking an accumulated rest and a medical team was present. The scene around him became something of a street party and videos from the event went viral across social media platforms, drawing more people to the venue. Moronumubo Akodu, who repeatedly visited to support Ben Dancer throughout the week, said she was impressed by his determination but worried about the physical toll. "It is actually insane, but I am so proud of him," she told the BBC. Image source, Saycheese Image caption, Crowds of people have gathered to watch the performance Emmanuel Ulelu, who visited the performance twice, said he noticed a striking change in the dancer's energy. "On day two, you could see the stress," he said. "Even after just three hours of dancing at the location myself, I wondered how he would keep going." But when he returned 16 hours into day five, he said Ben Dancer appeared more energetic than before. "It reminded me that we're capable of doing unbelievable things when how badly we want something matches and surpasses the difficulty of achieving it," he said. Nigeria has also developed a strong relationship with Guinness World Records, particularly in entertainment. In 2023, Nigerian chef Hilda Baci cooked continuously for 93 hours and 11 minutes in Lagos, which Guinness officially recognised as a new record. Her achievement sparked a surge of interest in record attempts in Nigeria, even though others have since surpassed her. Guinness says it received more than 1,500 new applications from the country within two months of her cook-a-thon, including events such as reading, singing, and crocheting. "It's been brilliant to see such strong enthusiasm for record breaking across Nigeria in recent years," a Guinness spokesperson told the BBC.
